title: What am I for?
hook: every life is called to love in its own way

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chief end: to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever. Your line was glorify and enjoy. Which mouthful did you slow down for? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

Night, in the temple of the LORD at Shiloh. A boy named Samuel is lying down, and the lamp hasn't gone out yet. He hears his name. He gets up and runs to the old priest, Eli: "Here am I; for thou calledst me." Eli says he didn't call. Go back to bed. It happens again. And again. Samuel keeps running to the wrong person. Finally Eli understands, and tells the boy what to say next time. When the voice comes, Samuel answers: "Speak; for thy servant heareth." Yesterday's question was what a human life is for. Today asks it smaller, and closer: what is my life for? Today's word: calling.
screen: `A BOY HEARS HIS NAME AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Calling. Paul's Greek word is klesis. Paul writes to the church in Corinth, people who were slaves and free, married and single, and says: "Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called." Calling, and called, side by side in one sentence. The ordinary life you're in when the call finds you can be the place where you answer it. Martin Luther and other reformers pressed this hard. A calling, they taught, isn't only for priests, monks and nuns. A farmer, a parent, a shoemaker can each have one. Catholic teaching speaks of a universal call to holiness: every baptized person, in whatever state of life. Orthodox writers speak of every life as a way toward God. The churches describe it differently, and the shared thread is that the call isn't kept for a few. So what is everyone called to? Paul gives one answer to the Galatians: "ye have been called unto liberty," and then he says what the freedom is for: "by love serve one another." Called, and the shape of it is love. Your own way of loving is the part that differs. One person's love looks like fixing things. Another's looks like listening, or teaching, or sitting up with a sick parent. And notice Samuel: he heard the call before he knew who was calling, and he kept running to the wrong person. Some readers find comfort in that. A calling can take more than one try, and sometimes another person, like old Eli, helps you hear it.

Here's the practice: name your calling in one line. Settle, and breathe. Don't think about job titles. Think about the people in your life, and the way you most often end up loving them. Fixing, feeding, listening, making them laugh, telling the truth. Let one line come, starting with: I am called to love by... and finish it yourself. If it doesn't come, that's all right; Samuel needed more than one call. If you pray, you can say Samuel's words, "Speak; for thy servant heareth," and then wait. The bell holds the time.
Calling. Klesis, Paul's word for it. In his letters, a call that finds people in ordinary lives, and whose shape is love.
Your line: called to love. Write your one line somewhere you'll see it, and do one small thing today that fits it. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Christians talk about calling, or vocation, in many settings: some churches pray for people in their daily work, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of callings to marriage, single life, priesthood and religious life.

original.note: Greek: a calling. Paul's word in abide in the same calling wherein he was called.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calling is something only priests and nuns get.
what it means: in Paul's letters, the call finds people in ordinary lives, and its shape is love: by love serve one another.
what a scholar hears: klesis, Paul's word for calling. the reformers used the idea to say a farmer's work could be a calling, and Catholic teaching speaks of a universal call to holiness.

notes: 'ye have been called unto liberty' is spoken from Galatians 5:13 KJV ('For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty'); confirm.
The hook places Samuel 'in the house of God at Shiloh' and says the lamp hadn't gone out (1 Samuel 3:3; Shiloh from 1 Samuel 1–3). Confirm.
Luther and the reformers on vocation (farmer, parent, shoemaker as examples) is stated as their teaching; confirm the examples are fair.
Catholic 'universal call to holiness' (Lumen Gentium ch. 5) and the Orthodox line ('every life as a way toward God') are brief summaries; Keeper to confirm.
Klesis from the verb kaleo (to call) is standard lexicon material; confirm.
1 Corinthians 7:20 is set in Paul's discussion of slaves and free, married and single (7:17–24); the script does not develop 7:21 (gaining freedom). Keeper may want a note.
